Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

Authorities also confirmed the four bears were not involved in that earlier attack, which injured 11 people.

Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. The release of water from the Cheakamus Dam flooded roads near Squamish and was intended to make room in the reservoir for more rain. Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. Rain eased in some areas, but Vancouver Island remained under rainfall and flood warnings, and forecasters were tracking more storm systems expected over the weekend.

items.title: [rabble.ca] Canadians rally nationwide against bill expanding fast-track project powers
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

More than 65 protests took place across Canada on Nov. 12 against Bill C-39, the federal Building Canada Strong Act, which would let Cabinet designate regions of “national interest” and accelerate approvals for major projects. The bill could cover pipelines, energy infrastructure and industrial developments and would set a one-year timeline for decisions on designated projects. Indigenous, environmental and labour groups argue the bill could weaken environmental safeguards, treaty rights and workers’ ability to strike; the federal government says it would speed up projects supporting economic growth and energy security while maintaining Indigenous consultation. A House of Commons committee is studying the bill, and a special Senate committee is conducting a pre-study; no date for its final House vote has been publicly announced.

items.title: [energynow.com] Norway’s Supreme Court invalidates three oilfield permits over emissions reviews
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Norway’s Supreme Court on Nov. 13 invalidated government approvals for the North Sea oilfields Breidablikk, Tyrving and Yggdrasil, ruling that environmental reviews should have assessed emissions from burning the extracted oil, not just from production. The six-to-five decision requires the Energy Ministry to reconsider the permits under proper procedures but does not order operators to stop work. Equinor’s Breidablikk and Aker BP’s Tyrving are producing, and Yggdrasil is scheduled to start production in 2027. Environmental groups Greenpeace Norway and Young Friends of the Earth brought the case against the state in 2023. The court said the oil companies were not parties to the case, so the ruling does not automatically suspend their operations. The campaigners’ lawyer said they would consider bringing a separate case against the operators. The ministry said it would re-examine the permits. The government has said it has changed its practice to include emissions from burning oil and gas in assessments for new fields.

items.title: [cisa.gov] U.S. agencies warn hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration controls
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Five U.S. agencies warned on Nov. 5 that hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide, including controllers used by grocery stores, hospitals, food producers and transport operators. Attackers may exploit unpatched or internet-accessible devices to change temperatures or defrost settings, or prevent operators from seeing temperature readings. Such attacks could spoil stock, compromise storage safety and damage equipment. The warning follows attacks on European supermarkets on Nov. 2 and an incident that altered refrigeration settings at three French blood-service facilities. The U.S. agencies did not say whether refrigeration systems in the United States had been targeted. They urged operators to remove unnecessary internet access, secure remote connections, update firmware, isolate control systems from business networks and set alerts for unsafe temperature changes.

items.title: [bleepingcomputer.com] Attack on French blood-service contractor reaches refrigeration controls
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

An attack on a refrigeration service provider used by France’s national blood service reached monitoring and control systems at three sites on Nov. 2. The blood service said it was not directly targeted. Investigators have not publicly identified how attackers entered the contractor’s systems, which control equipment was affected or who was responsible. French reporting said attackers set controls to request temperatures as high as 110°C, but that figure does not establish the temperatures reached inside storage units or blood products. European retailers have also faced attacks on internet-connected refrigeration controls. Interface cybersecurity adviser Sven Herpig said the supermarket attacks exploited weak or known credentials and a lack of multi-factor authentication, while another security expert pointed to default passwords and outdated systems. Investigators have not confirmed that the blood-storage attack exploited the same weaknesses or was linked to the retail incidents. The European Commission, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) and other EU bodies advised organizations to act immediately to reduce exposure and are sharing information with national authorities. Under the EU Cyber Resilience Act, manufacturers have been required to report severe incidents and actively exploited vulnerabilities since Sept. 11, 2026. Its main security requirements take effect Dec. 11, 2027.

items.title: [traficom.fi] Cyberattacks disrupt refrigeration, water and energy control systems
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Cyber incidents targeting operational technology (OT) systems—the controllers that monitor and operate physical equipment—have disrupted refrigeration, water and energy operations, often through exposed or outdated devices. Attacks on European supermarket refrigeration systems caused food spoilage, while incidents affecting U.S. water utilities and Polish energy organizations disrupted monitoring and control. French industry estimates put food waste and structural damage from the refrigeration attacks at tens of millions of euros. Isolating a compromised system can cut operators off from equipment-status information they need to make safe decisions, according to a Communications of the ACM contributor. Finland’s Transport and Communications Agency said household smart devices were not targets in the European refrigeration attacks, but advised users to secure routers and connected devices.

items.title: [tsln.com] Cattle specialists urge targeted winter feeding to manage costs
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Cattle advisers and researchers are urging producers to match winter rations to forage quality and herd needs. Drought has tightened forage supplies, and feed is a major operating expense. South Dakota State University research found that limit-fed, energy-dense diets reduced feed use and methane emissions without harming calf growth through weaning, saving about $29 per cow. Kansas State University cow-calf specialist Jason Warner recommends assessing forage and supplementing protein as dormant grasses lose quality. French livestock trainer Guillaume Beaure describes reducing feed waste by closely matching rations to animals’ needs. Advisers also recommend checking forage mineral levels because winter hay can pose a risk of magnesium deficiency.

The new study is the first major test of whether it could supplant BMI—and the results are encouraging. The 2025 _Lancet_ study recommended supplementing BMI with measurements such as waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio to better identify excess body fat. It also proposed assessing whether that fat was causing measurable organ dysfunction. In the new study, by analyzing health data from more than 844,000 adults across four countries, the researchers found that BMI both overestimated and underestimated obesity in certain groups compared with the new framework. They also found that people with clinical and preclinical obesity faced markedly different long-term health risks. items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A cyberattack on a refrigeration provider disrupted cold-storage controls at three French blood-bank sites on Nov. 2, raising temperature and defrost thresholds to dangerous levels, the French Blood Establishment (EFS) said. Monitoring and alarm systems detected the changes, and staff took precautions, including moving some products. The incident was part of a wave of attacks on refrigeration systems that disrupted European supermarkets in October. Sweden’s regions said no comparable blood-bank attack had been reported there, but they were reviewing and strengthening cybersecurity protections. French authorities said technical investigations were continuing to determine how the breach occurred, how many devices may have been affected and when the systems could safely return to service.

The United Nations World Food Programme warns that it could push 49 million more people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, bringing the total to 274 million. Drought has already cut rainfall in northern Sudan to less than half of normal, while dry conditions are affecting crops, livestock and transport in parts of Central America and Southeast Asia. The Famine Early Warning Systems Network projects that 2026-27 production of maize, wheat and rice will be 2.7% below the previous year but still the second-largest on record. El Niño is forecast to peak in December and persist into early 2027. In the Philippines, forecasters expect below-normal rainfall in November and drought conditions in several provinces.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN-backed report warns overshooting 1.5C could permanently damage Earth's ice
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

Security researchers found that 35,578 of 37,571 web apps built with SpaceXSI’s Grok Build, a chat-based app builder, were accessible without signing in, exposing business and personal information at SpaceXSI and 30 other organizations. Claroc, the security firm that found the apps, estimated that about one in 10 accessible apps contained internal or personal data and roughly 2% held material it rated high or critical in severity. The apps’ addresses were discoverable through searchable passive DNS records, and Grok Build preselected “Anyone with the link” as the sharing option in the researchers’ test. SpaceXSI removed 24 apps made by its own staff and X employees; Claroc said other users’ apps remained available and that it had begun contacting affected organizations.

items.title: [al-monitor.com] US sanctions eight Canadian currency firms over alleged Iran transfers
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The U.S. Treasury on Nov. 6 sanctioned eight money-services businesses in Ontario and British Columbia, alleging they moved funds for Iran and sanctioned Iranian entities, including by converting Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets. The businesses are Million Exchange, Amin Exchange, Top PC Technician, NIA Nations Currency, Farah Exchange, CCC Inc., Cryptoyal and Darvish Exchange. The sanctions block any assets they hold under U.S. jurisdiction and bar U.S. persons and entities from transacting with them. U.S. officials also said several firms handled money for Ryan Wedding, a Canadian former Olympic snowboarder and alleged drug-trafficking figure. The Treasury accused three firms of laundering drug proceeds by converting bulk cash into digital assets. The action was coordinated with the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC), Canada’s financial intelligence agency, and U.S. agencies. Separately, the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the U.S. anti-money-laundering unit, barred U.S. financial institutions from processing transfers involving MEXC Global, a cryptocurrency exchanger incorporated in Seychelles. FinCEN said MEXC facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions linked to Iran, North Korea and Russia, as well as other sanctioned actors.

items.title: [aa.com.tr] Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi cruise missile aimed at Riyadh
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a Houthi cruise missile aimed at Riyadh on Saturday, the latest reported attack in renewed cross-border fighting between the coalition and Yemen’s Houthi movement. On Friday, coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said air defenses destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward Najran. Debris fell, and authorities began assessing damage. The coalition also reported intercepting drones in the Makkah and Riyadh regions. The Houthis have repeatedly denied targeting Makkah or Madinah and say their operations target oil infrastructure and military sites. The latest interceptions follow the breakdown of a truce in July and renewed fighting in Yemen, where government forces have sought to retake territory from the Houthis.

items.title: [simon42.com] AI tool HA-MCP arrives in the Home Assistant Marketplace and requires admin privileges
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The community project HA-MCP can be installed directly through the integrated Marketplace starting with Home Assistant 2026.11. It connects AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT to Home Assistant and enables not only device control but also the creation and modification of automations, scripts, and dashboards. Previously, installation required a separate HACS entry. With version 9.0.0 on October 28, the server was integrated into Home Assistant. HA-MCP requires administrator privileges; the developers recommend a separate account restricted to local access. Remote access and access from the home network are initially disabled. For Home Assistant 2026.8 through 2026.10, HACS remains the installation method.

items.title: [simon42.com] AVM rolls out FRITZ!OS 8.51 and no longer sends the DNS suffix “fritz.box” by default via DHCP
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Since November 3, AVM has been rolling out FRITZ!OS 8.51 to additional FRITZ!Box models and the Repeater 6000. By default, the box no longer sends the DNS suffix “fritz.box” via DHCP. This can affect the accessibility of Home Assistant installations and other devices on the home network if they are accessed using a short hostname such as “homeassistant” rather than an IP address or a fully qualified address. Home Assistant OS 18.5 has also been released. The security update upgrades the Linux kernel on Raspberry Pi and Home Assistant Yellow to version 6.18.59 and fixes a vulnerability in IPv4 network processing. The fix was already included in version 18.4 for other boards. The developers particularly recommend the update for Raspberry Pis that are directly accessible from the internet or run on untrusted networks.
